Mayo Clinic News Network stated on October 11, 2021, that assertions about microchips in COVID-19 vaccines are false, and there is no way for the vaccine to track people or gather personal information. [1] This myth originated from comments made by Bill Gates about a digital certificate of vaccine records, which was not a microchip and was not implemented in COVID-19 vaccines. [1] Mayo Clinic further clarified on August 30, 2026, that COVID-19 vaccines are made only with ingredients that help the body recognize and clear out the virus, and it is a myth that they contain microchips to track location or movement. [2] FactCheck.org reported on December 15, 2020, that a video falsely claiming COVID-19 vaccine vials have a microchip to track patients misrepresented an interview about a chip attached to a plastic vial to store information about the vaccine dose, not to track people. [3] KSAT reported on January 12, 2021, that local medical experts in San Antonio warned about the prevalence of misinformation, including the unfounded social media theory that COVID-19 vaccines contain microchips and tracking devices, which they determined to be untrue. [4] AFP Fact Check stated on July 2, 2021, that social media posts claiming COVID-19 vaccines contain trackers are false, and health authorities confirm no chip is in any vaccine product. [5] Jala Hoaks Jakarta, on January 21, 2021, and CSIRT Bulelengkab, on March 7, 2026, both clarified that claims of COVID-19 vaccines containing chips to track people are false, explaining that barcodes on vaccine products are for tracking distribution, not individuals.
